chapter: Dallas bands, Ray Charles and family
title: The chicken dance act exposes Boston at the Rose Room
summary: At the Rose Room the dancer's piano music exposed Boston's inability to read; Smith rewrote it on alto.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: You told me that wonderful story about the woman dressed up as a chicken.
Can you tell me that one again?

Yeah. It was one of them acts coming at... That's what I was telling him. I said, "Boston, one .....(?)...... where you were last night." You see how he's playing piano. You always tell a man that can't read music, his chords sound different, because he ain't had... In other words, he hasn't studied. See, whatever you do, if you study, practice makes perfect, and you'll be good on it. But see, he ain't gonna to study. He ain't gonna play nothin' but the blues. He wouldn't care if he's playing for the President of the United States in the White House; he'd go in there and sit down on the piano and go playing the blues! Heh-heh-heh. Just that stupid. He's my brother and I love him, but he's just that stupid. So I've been

1943! When I first opened my little band up here... Up here in the Log Cabin, right up here in Queen City. Eight pieces up there. And he was in the band, and I wrote some numbers and names around him. We was working up at that Rose Room, that big fine club... That big White woman, a big race horse woman -- she ran the place. We was playing there, and they'd bring them shows in.

But this one had the Ticklettes(?), come out of New York, and a girl was dancing who was dressed like...just like a chicken. Just like a rooster. Looked like a rooster up there. And she had some music stretched clean across the front of the piano. And nothing but the piano. Just the piano and the drums going along with her. And we hadn't rehearsed that evening. She threw that music up there and everything, and that pulled the cover off of everything. And the boss lady wanted to see what kind of dance the girls were gonna do where they're all dressed like a chicken up there and all that stuff, and she wanted to hear that music and see what it was. And she noticed, she caught on that my brother was reading the music, couldn't read the music. He couldn't play it.
So how did you handle it? She came to you or what?
So the girl said, 'Buster, your brother's not

playing the music right. He's can't play it." He said, "Well, I can't see that. My eyes bad. I can't see that." She said, "I've got to work. Somebody got to play my act. You got to play." So the boss lady was sitting down there on the chair right there on the bandstand, looking. She said, "Buster, do you mean to tell me I've been paying this brother of yours all this much money all this long time, and that man can't read no music?" I said, "Oh yeah, he can read it, Miss Holt, but he's just a little slow. I'll tell you what to do to make it sound better, and I'll fix it up to where it can come out all right."

So I kind of talked to the girl, and I take the music and carried it around the corner there to my girlfriend's house, and sat down all of the evenin', the rest of the evenin', and wrote it out and played it on my alto. And he followed me on the alto. That's the only thing he did. And I just played all the technical parts in there.
Yeah, and he just played the chords.
